 caret-right News | Elections New Zealand’s governing coalition holds slim majority in preliminary count
 New Zealand’s National and Labour parties each secure just short of 30 percent of the popular vote. 
 Listen Listen (4 mins) Save
 Share New Zealand’s governing coalition holds slim majority in preliminary count on social media share-nodes Share
 facebook x whatsapp-stroke copylink google Add Al Jazeera on Google info Supporters cheer at the election party of Christopher Luxon, leader of the National Party, in Auckland, New Zealand, on November 7, 2026 [David Rowland/Reuters] By Al Jazeera Staff , AFP and Reuters Published On 7 Nov 2026 7 Nov 2026 New Zealand’s National-led coalition has a slim majority in preliminary election results, but with about 14 percent of votes still to be counted, it is unclear who will govern the country for the next three years.
 Preliminary results from the Electoral Commission on Sunday showed the governing coalition of the National Party, ACT and New Zealand First with 67 of a projected 131 seats, one more than the 66 needed for a majority.
 The commission said special votes, about 14 percent of the total vote, remain to be counted. These votes, which include ballots from New Zealanders overseas and people voting outside their electorate, have historically favoured the left.
 They will be released with the final result on November 27. Until then, the coalition will continue as a caretaker government.
 Neither Prime Minister Christopher Luxon nor Labour Party and Opposition Leader Chris Hipkins claimed victory in their election-night speeches, in a campaign dominated by a soft economy and the cost of living.
 Simeon Brown, a National lawmaker and campaign chair, told public broadcaster TVNZ the party was in “a strong position”. “We feel quite confident at this stage we can form a government, a National-led government, with our coalition partners,” he said.
 The Electoral Commission also said on Saturday that the centrist Opportunity Party will meet the 5 percent threshold to enter parliament. If the coalition loses its majority in the final count, either it or a left-leaning coalition would need the support of Opportunity.
 Advertisement Luxon has repeatedly ruled out working with Opportunity, but Brown said on Sunday that he was not ruling out talks with the centrist party.
 “National is once again the largest party in parliament, and we have a pathway to forming the next government,” Luxon told supporters in Auckland on Sunday. “But right now, it is too close to call.”
 Hipkins, the opposition leader, told supporters: “New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you’ve said.
 “Our next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together, and to find common ground.”
 Polling stations opened at 9am on Saturday (20:00 GMT Friday) and closed at 7pm (06:00 GMT Saturday). There is no timeframe for when a government must be formed.
 Supporters gather at Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins’s election night watch party, in Upper Hutt, New Zealand, on November 7, 2026 [Hollie Adams/Reuters] ‘Interparty negotiations’ expected
 New Zealand’s 2026 election was at times dubbed the “supermarket election”, as grocery prices and supermarket competition became a key battleground for the parties.
 Peter Dunne, a former member of parliament who also served as a minister in both National and Labour-led governments, said the election was “much more of a cost-of-living election”, with voters essentially looking at “which of the main blocs is better placed to ease the cost of living burden on New Zealanders”.
 “The ruling coalition appears well ahead of the centre-left. Now, that may change, because these are early results, but it’s a little bit of a surprise that this is happening,” Dunne told Al Jazeera. “We were looking to a much tighter contest than appears to be the case at the moment.”
 The National Party pledged to return the budget to surplus through fiscal discipline while expanding the national pension scheme. The Labour Party promised cheaper healthcare and transport.
 The former minister added that both main parties are practically “carbon copies of the other”, leaving “a whole rising generation of voters, who want to see a bit more adventure in politics”.
 Therefore, Dunne said, the results show support rallying behind other parties, like “strong support for the Green Party, the right-wing libertarian [ACT New Zealand], the xenophobic nationalist [New Zealand First] party, and a new centrist party, the Opportunity Party, which wants to be in the middle between all of them”.
 He told Al Jazeera that even though the Opportunity Party is hovering around 5 percent at the moment, “it’s been one of the big stars of this campaign”.
 Political party billboards in a suburb of Wellington, New Zealand, on October 31, 2026 [Charlotte Graham-McLay/AP] Dunne told Al Jazeera that if both main parties “end up relatively evenly placed, then the onus could go on the Opportunity Party”.
 Advertisement “If Opportunity Party reaches parliament, it will talk to the largest party first, which appears to be the National Party, but there’s no guarantee that they could come to an arrangement,” he said.
 “We could face weeks of interparty negotiations to form a government. Parliament has to sit by early January, so there’s a real prospect that we could go into Christmas with no clear government in New Zealand,” Dunne added.
 New Zealand holds a general election every three years under a mixed-member proportional system, which means most governments are coalitions.
 Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.
